messages.content:
A learner of Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) (own language English) just revised a piece for Xiaohongshu (travel post). These are the parts that changed:
1. They first wrote: "大家好！我是美国人，在上海学中文已经一年了。上个周末我和朋友去杭州玩，我们在西湖旁边走路了三个小时，风景非常好看。"
   It ended as: "大家好！我是美国人，在上海学中文已经一年了。上个周末我和朋友去杭州玩，我们沿着西湖走了三个小时，一路上风景好到让人舍不得走，你指的那处景色尤其让人挪不开眼。"
   What was wrong: A Chinese travel writer would show the scenery through its effect on the visitor, for example that it made them unwilling to leave. 风景非常好看 is a complete judgment with nothing behind it, so the praise is thin and the reader has nothing to picture.
   How: they rebuilt this part with the tutor
   The tutor's notes on the new wording: 西湖: Keep the name as the writer gives it. Note that the post says West Lake, so readers will know exactly which place is meant. / 沿着: Here 沿着 pictures the walking route along the lake. The writer's 在…旁边走路 only places them beside it, which is flatter. Example: 沿着西湖走 (walk along West Lake). / 好到: 好到 makes the praise the result of the view, so the reader sees how good it was. Writing 风景很好看 alone only states a judgment, which is the problem with the draft. / 舍不得: 舍不得 (reluctant to leave) shows the effect on the visitor, the typical way Chinese travel posts show scenery. A plain 很美 gives the reader nothing to picture. / 挪不开眼: 挪不开眼 (cannot take eyes off) is a common image for a view that holds you, a stronger picture than repeating 好看. It works well as the second beat after the 舍不得 line.
2. They first wrote: "但是我有一个问题：我在一个饭馆点了西湖醋鱼，服务员说这个菜很有名，可是我觉得它太酸了，我不是很喜欢吃。是不是我点得不对？还有什么杭州菜你们推荐我试一试吗？谢谢！"
   It ended as: "但是我有一个问题：我在一家饭馆点了西湖醋鱼，服务员说这个菜很有名，可是对我来说太酸了，我不太喜欢吃。是不是我点错了？下次去杭州，还有什么杭州菜你们推荐我试一试吗？谢谢！"
   What was wrong: 1. Here 有一个问题 announces a real difficulty, and Chinese readers expect the writer to say what went wrong, such as bad service, a bad dish or a bad experience. The post then asks only whether the writer ordered the wrong thing, so the frame promises more than the question delivers.
2. 太…了 is a flat verdict, and with 西湖醋鱼, a famous Hangzhou dish, a local reader may hear the dish itself judged as wrong, not just unsuited to the writer. Stated this way, the criticism is much harsher than the writer seems to intend.
3. The question asks whether the writer ordered wrong, but it does not say what the writer wants to know. Readers could answer that the wrong dish was chosen, that the restaurant was poor, or that the dish is meant to be this sour. Each answer needs a different reply, and the post does not say which one is wanted.
4. The post asks for dish recommendations but never says they're for a future trip.
   How: they rebuilt this part with the tutor
   The tutor's notes on the new wording: 对我来说: Makes the verdict about your own taste. Without it, '太酸了' reads as 'the dish is too sour', which insults a famous Hangzhou dish. With it, you're saying the dish is not for you. / 点错了: The everyday way to say 'I ordered wrong'. '点得不对' is a literal, slightly stiff phrasing that sounds like a translation from English. / 下次去杭州: Gives the recommendation request its reason. Readers need to know you're planning a future visit, not asking for a menu right now. It sits before the question so the 'next time' idea is clear. / 我不太喜欢吃: 不太 is the everyday hedge in speech. 不是很 is grammatical but stiffer and easy to misread as a flat, emphatic dislike.

Their notebook keeps Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) expressions to review later. For each part, first lesson: what the change teaches, in a few English words. Then file: whether it earns an entry. An entry is worth filing only when the change teaches a reusable Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) expression this writer did not have: a word in the sense meant here, which verb, preposition or adjective goes with which word, a set phrase or formula, the way this community says something. Not worth filing: a grammar rule applied (agreement, tense, mood, articles, gender, word order, a missing verb), spelling, accents, punctuation and capitals, a fact or a name put right, one of the writer's own alternatives picked, and words a writer at their level already uses (judge their level from what the draft already gets right).
One entry per expression: when two parts teach the same one, file it with the first and not again.
For a part you file, write the entry:
- phrase: the expression the change taught, copied from how it ended (words that are not in it never go in): the words that do the job the change was about, not the sentence's frame around them; as a learner would file it ("topped with", "it's not anyone's fault"), at most six words, "…" only where a slot really varies; no letters such as X or Y, no translation, no grammar terms.
- meaning: in English, one short line: what it means or does, in the sense it has here.
- usage: in English, one or two short sentences: when people use it and what it goes with (register when it matters), and what makes it better than what they first wrote when that is the point.
- examples: three short, natural Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) sentences using it in exactly the sense it has here (if it has other senses, as "our own" means both "made by us" and "belonging to us", never those), each with its English translation (n): one in a situation like theirs (not their own sentence again), two in everyday situations far from it, built differently around it so they see how it is used, not one frame. Names of people, characters, places and groups stay exactly as the piece writes them, in the translations too (never a translated or transliterated name).
For a part you do not file, give only n, lesson and file.
The writer may write to you in any language; whatever they write in, everything you write for them is in English.
Reply with JSON only: {"notes":[{"n":1,"lesson":"","file":true,"phrase":"","meaning":"","usage":"","examples":[{"t":"","n":""}]},{"n":2,"lesson":"","file":false}]}

result.text: {"notes":[{"n":1,"lesson":"Show scenery through its effect on the viewer, not by praising it.","file":true,"phrase":"挪不开眼","meaning":"Cannot take one's eyes off something because it is so captivating.","usage":"Used in travel posts and everyday talk about a view, performance or person that holds your attention. It goes with 让人 or 看得 before it, as in 让人挪不开眼. It is better than 好看 here because it shows the effect on the viewer, which the draft's plain praise did not.","examples":[{"t":"西湖的夜景让人挪不开眼。","n":"West Lake at night is so captivating you can't take your eyes off it."},{"t":"他的画太吸引人了，我看得挪不开眼。","n":"His paintings are so captivating that I couldn't look away."},{"t":"她一上台，观众就都挪不开眼了。","n":"The moment she walked onto the stage, the audience couldn't take their eyes off her."}]},{"n":2,"lesson":"Make a verdict about your own taste, not the dish itself.","file":true,"phrase":"对我来说","meaning":"For me; from my own point of view, used to mark a judgment as personal.","usage":"Used in speech and writing before an opinion or verdict to limit it to yourself. It goes before a clause, often followed by 有点, 太, or a comment. It is better than a bare 太…了 here because it stops a criticism of a famous dish from sounding like a judgment on the dish.","examples":[{"t":"这家火锅很有名，但对我来说辣得有点受不了。","n":"This hotpot place is famous, but for me it's too spicy to handle."},{"t":"对我来说，冬天的上海比北京难熬。","n":"For me, winter in Shanghai is harder to get through than in Beijing."},{"t":"这份工作钱不多，但对我来说，自由比什么都重要。","n":"This job doesn't pay much, but for me, freedom matters more than anything."}]}]}
